Welcome to the farm

Farming the way it has always been done — with patience, care and muddy boots.

Ours is a small, family-run mixed farm in the British countryside, where livestock graze the pastures and the fields are worked in step with the seasons. Nothing here is rushed and nothing is done by halves: animals are known as individuals, soil is treated as something borrowed from the next generation, and the harvest is shared with the community around us.

We supply neighbours, local shops and businesses with honest farm produce, and we are always glad to hear from people who care about where their food comes from.

  • 01

  • 02

Our farming · Animal husbandry

Livestock, looked after properly.

Animal farming is at the heart of this concept. The picture the family has in mind is cattle grazing the lower pastures, sheep keeping the hill fields trimmed and hens scratching about in the open air — each animal raised slowly, outdoors, and with genuine respect.

Good husbandry is not complicated: space, fresh grass, clean water, shelter when the weather turns, and a stockperson who notices when something is not quite right. That is the standard aimed for here, every day of the year.

Example content — the livestock described is illustrative; the family will confirm the final details before launch.

  • Grass-fed grazing — livestock rotated around the pastures so the land rests as they move.
  • Free-ranging stock — animals out on the grass by day, shut in safely against the fox by night.
  • Daily checks, always — every animal seen, fed and watered by a member of the family.
  • Raised slowly — no rushing growth; animals mature at their own natural pace.
From our fieldsVegetables and cereals grown in rotation and harvested at their best.
Our farming · Crop cultivation

Seasonal crops, grown with the year.

The arable side of the farm works to the rhythm of the British year: sowing in spring, watching the crops through summer, and bringing in the harvest before the autumn rains. Fields are rotated between vegetables, cereals and grass so the soil is never asked for more than it can give.

Everything is picked and gathered when it is ready — not before — which is why farm produce tastes the way it should.

SpringSowing, planting out and the first salads
SummerSoft fruit, new potatoes and sweetcorn
AutumnHarvest, orchard fruit and roots
WinterLeeks, brassicas and stores from the barn
  • Crop rotation — fields rest and recover between crops, with grass leys in the mix.
  • Fed by the farm — muck from the livestock goes back onto the land, closing the loop.
  • Picked at its peak — harvested by hand where it matters and sold close to home.

Our approach

Farming responsibly, in the plain sense of the word.

We do not deal in grand claims. Sustainability on a small farm is mostly ordinary good practice, repeated year after year: look after the soil, treat animals well, waste as little as possible, and leave the land in better heart than you found it.

i.

Care for the Land

Rotation, resting fields and returning muck to the soil keep the ground fertile without asking too much of it.

ii.

Welfare Before Yield

Animals are kept in conditions we would happily show anyone — space, grass, shelter and time to grow naturally.

iii.

Seasonal by Nature

We grow what suits the season and the soil, and we eat — and sell — what the farm is actually producing.

iv.

Food Miles Kept Low

Produce is sold locally wherever we can manage it: fewer miles, fresher food, and money staying in the community.

About us

A family farm, through and through.

Everything here is done by the family — the early-morning rounds, the school-run dash back for lambing, the long evenings of harvest. It is a way of life as much as a business, and we would not have it any other way.

Like many small British farms, ours has changed shape over the years: fields added, barns rebuilt, new ventures tried alongside the old certainties of livestock and crops. What has never changed is the belief that good farming is careful farming — of animals, of land, and of the people who eat what we produce.

Looking ahead, we want to welcome more of our neighbours to the farm gate, keep improving the health of our soil, and hand the whole thing on in good heart to whoever farms it next.

"We are only borrowing this land, really. The job is to leave it better than we found it."
